query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A diffusion‐based surface aluminization treatment will form a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer on the as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that serves as an effective oxygen diffusion barrier at 1000 °C, dramatically enhancing the alloy’s oxidation resistance while preserving its inherent room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a diffusion‐based surface aluminization treatment (e.g., by exposing the alloy to an aluminum-rich pack or gaseous environment at elevated temperature) to induce in-situ formation of a thin Al2O3 scale.
generation.conditions: The treatment and subsequent testing are conducted at around 1000 °C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere with exposure durations on the order of tens to hundreds of hours and under mechanical loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent, and thermodynamically stable alumina layer formed at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminization process promotes aluminum diffusion into the near-surface region, where it reacts with oxygen to form a protective alumina scale. This barrier inhibits further oxygen ingress, thereby reducing high-temperature oxidation without altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the alloy's mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the treated alloy will show significantly improved oxidation resistance at 1000 °C—with minimal weight gain and surface degradation—while maintaining 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength in the 163–530 MPa range at high temperature.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits poor oxygen resistance that limits its high-temperature performance despite its favorable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The intervention must be applied only as a surface treatment, preserving the as-cast bulk microstructure; it is intended to be effective specifically under high-temperature (≈1000 °C) conditions in an oxygen-rich environment and during testing at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise processing parameters (e.g., treatment temperature, time, and aluminum source concentration) needed to produce an optimal and uniform alumina scale without causing detrimental aluminide diffusion into the bulk or altering the as-cast microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy: one set undergoes the diffusion-based surface aluminization treatment while the other is left untreated. Both sets are then exposed to an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Following exposure, conduct oxidation analysis and mechanical testing (room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength measurements under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Weight gain and oxide layer thickness (via thermogravimetric analysis and microscopy)
Surface oxide composition and continuity (using SEM/EDS and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the aluminized samples do not exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate (i.e., similar weight gains and oxide scale discontinuities as the untreated samples) or if the surface treatment degrades the alloy’s mechanical performance by reducing its room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength beyond the reported ranges.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

frame.system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr cast alloy in its as‐cast microstructure
frame.goal: Enhance high‐temperature oxygen resistance to enable practical use at elevated temperatures while preserving its inherent room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at ~1000 °C)
frame.limitation: The alloy’s poor oxygen resistance, which restricts its use in high-temperature applications
constraints: A single intervention must be used
The intervention must not sacrifice the alloy’s mechanical performance (i.e., tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at 1000 °C)
The solution should be applicable to the as-cast state
Maintain operational strain rate conditions (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹)
frame.regime: High-temperature service conditions (around 1000 °C) in an oxygen-containing atmosphere with exposure times typical of intended high-temperature applications under tensile loading
prior_attempts: While not explicitly stated, previous approaches (e.g., minor compositional adjustments or microstructure modifications) likely compromised either mechanical properties or did not sufficiently improve oxygen resistance.
frame.hypothesis: A promising single intervention is to apply a diffusion-based surface aluminization treatment to the as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy. The mechanism is the formation of a thin, adherent, and thermodynamically stable Al₂O₃ (alumina) layer on the alloy surface, which acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier at high temperatures. This protective alumina scale should maintain the alloy’s bulk mechanical properties while preventing rapid oxidation. The hypothesis predicts that, relative to the untreated alloy, the aluminized sample will exhibit dramatically improved oxygen resistance during prolonged exposure (e.g., tens to hundreds of hours) at 1000 °C in an oxygen-rich environment, all without compromising room-temperature tensile ductility or high-temperature yield strength. A controlled falsification experiment would be to subject both the aluminized and untreated samples to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (in controlled oxygen partial pressures, at 1000 °C over a specified time) combined with mechanical testing at the predetermined strain rates. A lack of significant difference in oxidation behavior or a degradation of mechanical properties in the aluminized samples would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on refractory and high‐entropy alloys have largely focused on optimizing mechanical performance by tuning processing parameters (casting, HIP, powder metallurgy, SLM) and modifying bulk compositions to control phase formation. For instance, one study (PMC7513042) introduced in‐situ formation of ceramic reinforcements—including Al2O3 particles—to enhance both high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance, although such approaches tended to affect ductility or involve complex processing steps. Other works modified phases via alloying (e.g., small Cr or Hf additions) and thermal treatments to balance strength and ductility, but oxygen resistance as a surface-limited issue remained unaddressed without compromising the favorable as-cast microstructure.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge is to overcome the alloy’s poor oxygen resistance in high-temperature, oxygen-rich environments without altering its inherent as-cast microstructure and mechanical properties (i.e., room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength). Bulk interventions or compositional modifications have not adequately decoupled oxidation resistance improvement from adverse effects on ductility and performance.
decision.lever: Diffusion-based surface aluminization treatment to form a thin, adherent, and thermodynamically stable alumina (Al2O3) scale
decision.why: This next step directly addresses oxygen ingress by modifying only the surface, thereby preserving the alloy’s bulk mechanical integrity. It builds on insights from earlier research that demonstrated the protective nature of alumina in high-temperature conditions while avoiding the pitfalls of bulk compositional changes or microstructural modifications that might degrade ductility. Controlling parameters such as treatment temperature (around or slightly below 1000 °C), exposure time (tens to hundreds of hours), and oxygen partial pressure during treatment is critical to achieve an optimal alumina layer that serves as an oxygen diffusion barrier without compromising the desirable mechanical properties.
